*Naelear*, those of the breath. Seren sets the word beside the sign, and the sign stays.
:::
It was the air we breathed.

Flat lay our land under the trees, past all measuring, to the far edge of the world. In their long sleep the trees breathed, and their breath lay down grey among the trunks. It fed the trees, and it fed us, and we tended it as ye tend a hearth.
Through the breath the sun came softened: the between-light, neither day nor dusk. For that light were we made, and never were we children of the dark.

At evening the light went low among the trunks. Then we sang to the pale saplings, and they answered, one stand and then the next, till the deep wood was one choir. Our little ones lay down among the roots to hear it. One by one their small voices left the song, and they slept in the singing.
Ferns of the deep wood, cast on bare sand, wither in the open sun. So wither we.
In the years of the iron we saw the open sun wither our children.
All our long summers we led the wood, root to water, and where we led it, there it grew. One life it was, in two kinds, and the wood kept its own will besides.

Without the breath the wood is sick. Without the wood the breath cometh not again. Without either we fail, and slowly, for we live twice as long as ye, and half again: the eldest last, and the youngest first.
Among the twisted boughs we kept our rites, and under the silver elders our council, for none lie beneath a silver elder.
Our speech is the storm in the high boughs, all cracks and breaks. Soft is all we carve. The thunder is for the moment, the softness for always.
What is carved is not heard but known: lay a hand on it, and ye know what the carver meant, whatever tongue he spake.
We wist not that there was any other way to be believed.

At the very edge, where the breath came down to your sea, stood our pillars in their long ranks. Between them they held the breath, as a mast holdeth a sail. We call them the Naelsaen, the mist-hearts: the anchors of our sky, and the only trees of ours ye ever found.
From among them we watched your shore, summer on summer. We saw your havens raised. We saw your lamps lit at dusk. We saw your boats come a little way in, and turn back.
Once a boat came farther than any. So near it came that we heard the oars stop. A man stood up in the bow and looked full at us.
We wove the breath thicker.
He saw but grey. His face went white, and the oars went back the way they came.
We wist not why.
Here is our fault, and the grain will not leave it out. We went not down to your shore. We hid, and were glad. So long hid we, and so well, that never once were we seen.
Since your first haven we had listened to you. Ye had never once heard us. We had made sure of it.

This is our home: the flat wood under the breath, the between-light, the pale saplings singing at evening, the silver elders at council. And at the edge of the world, the pillars, with the breath held up between them.
If any green be left of us, it remembereth this; and the grain holds it still.

t-II-3.book: **Rhyna.** So the Bonded die together, and we two fear it not. If one of a pair be killed, there is no wound on the other, and no sickness. But broken is the heart, for it knoweth. Still is the body, for its work is done. Eight days, men say, is the longest that ever one lived on alone. Hours, say the Stonewrights, that keep the count. Many have drawn their last breath in the same moment, a mile apart, and each wist that the other was going. And each went too. When the left hand dies, does not the right one die too?

t-II-3.book: **Halvard.** So she lived, and she is one. "A net is only knots holding hands," Tarnel told her, and with his knot is this Book bound. The wood she cannot know, for a knowing is held as two hands hold a stone that one cannot lift. But she will not die of another's death, and she can go where we two cannot, alone, and carry this Book on after us. Every scribe before her was of a pair, and when a pair went, their book went into the vault behind them. A book that none telleth is but ink. Look, her pen is not stopped. This Book must outlive its tellers. That is why it is Seren that writeth it.

t-IV-2.book:
::: note
Two marks of the wood's shape that {{Halyna}} could see, and could not yet tell
The first is the pillars, many, with a memory cut through them to the heart: *What one pillar felt, all the ranks felt, root to root.* The second is the mouth, mirrored, and tied back across the rings to the plea cut on the stone: *It did not answer.*
:::
This is held in the grain.
At the edge of the breath we stood in our long ranks, tall and dark of bark. We held the breath to the earth, as roots hold a bank.
Of that we thought not, for none think of breath till it be taken. We were the living pillars of the breath. For that alone we stood, and it was enough.
From the edge we watched your shore, and every hull of yours that came nigh us we marked. Each brush was a cut, and each trespass a wound. The wood keepeth every count.
In the high summer of your havens came the iron, in boats with many oars. Up out of the surf waded the shore-men.
What one pillar felt, all the ranks felt, root to root, to the far edge of the wood.
The first they came to stood nearest your shore. Of all the ranks it had marked the most of your hulls.
At first light they set the iron to it. Stroke on stroke it went in, and every stroke we counted. Ere noon it leaned. Yet it held the breath.
Then the roots let go.
Where it had stood, the sky came through, as daylight through a rent in a sail. It was pale.
One fell, and another. Summer after summer the shore-men came, till they that first brought the iron were old, and sent their sons. Then it was pale and hard.
The stumps put up shoots, straight and black, and in a few summers a young pillar stood where the old one fell. The iron came back for the young ones. We put up more. It came again.
Then it was pale and hard and wide.
The young of the long-lived turned their faces from the open sky, and wist not why they wept.
We carved, as ever we had carved when a thing must not be mistaken. But never laid the shore-men a hand on wood to know it. They cut it, and bare it away over the water.
So on the mute thing we cut our plea: on the stone your builders love, of which ye make your houses and your walls. For a people, we thought, must know best what is cut in the thing it loveth.

We cut it in our own soft letters. Where we had caught a word of yours across the water, that too we cut, as near its sound as our letters would go. At the feet of the pillars yet standing we set the stones.
All the made things of ours speak, and so we believed that all made things speak. It was a child's belief. Stone hath no mind.
It did not answer.

With the timber the shore-men took the stones away, and whither they went we wist not. At the last, along the whole edge, the stumps put up nothing, and the breath grew thin. We held our sap, and waited.
The iron will tire; and when it stoppeth, the wood will come again.
In the years of the iron we that tell you this were never a pillar. A thin green thing were we, at the edge.
Where the iron first went in, a stump was cut low, and we were its last shoot. In our rings lay the whole of the axe. The iron passed us over, for we were too thin to make a pole.

Forty summers had we stood when the long-lived of the council came seeking hearts, to bear their carvings. Not the straightest young tree chose they, nor the eldest. They chose us, for the axe in our rings.
When one of our hulls is struck, we go to the stroke, as the tongue to a broken tooth. It is in the rings.

t-IV-4.book: *— the blade — [ ]*
This is held in the grain.

Eldest wood are we. A tree we were when the world was green to its edges. We fell, and the ages lay down on us, leaf on leaf, till time forgat us and we grew dark and hard. Ye took us for stone. We are not stone.
Wood that time forgat forgetteth not. Slow is its giving, and true. Of all the gifts the long-lived give, the dearest is a sliver of such wood. We were given once.

Aelrhen he was named when he took his errand: bond-to-stone. A long life he listened across the breath, to the shore-men at their nets and at their walls. He gathered your words as a child gathereth fallen leaves, one and one and one. At the end he had three, and knew them for the right ones. Join them he could not. Ye join your words with small words, and small words make no sound across water.
But he had us. Whoso held us while a tree's shadow moved the breadth of its own trunk would know the whole of it. We were the sentence.

He chose the outermost of your holds, for its doors and its benches were of our wood. He took that for reverence. We knew it for what it was: our kin from the edge, sawn and polished. At the door he laid his hand on the post and greeted them. They answered not. They were dead.

He kneeled on the stones before the master of that house, and set us down. They that come under a roof bring their best, and we were his best. In the thunder of his own tongue he spake the name of the rite, *Ael'thar*, and after it his three words, in yours.
"Stop… Sky… Dying…"
A foot struck us into the dust by the wall. Laughter came to us through the dust.
He stopped not.

He rose, and took the back of the host's neck in his right hand, there where life goeth up into thought. A fledgling could have slept in that hand. The foreheads met, thought to thought, and he was silent.
With his left hand he set the blade to the host's arm.
And the host drew back. We know not why. Fear leaveth no mark on wood.
The blade that was to go a little way went deep, for the arm was moving. The host cried out, and his men came.
Then Aelrhen's blood ran over the stones of the step to where we lay, and with it came all of him: his long listening, and his last hour. So we know it as he knew it.

Between their hands he went down on his knees again, there where the rite began. He knew the blows as trees know the iron: one, and another. He lifted not his hand. The cut he would have made on his own arm was never made. He would ask no blood that he gave not. He gave it all, there on the step.
Never were the two arms laid together, shoulder to shoulder, that harm to the one should be harm to both. He died there, with the rite half made.
We lay in the dust and heard all of it, and no hand took us up. Of all things that ever lay at a shore-man's feet and looked like stone, we were the one that could have spoken to him.
And we were the one his foot found.
In the morning a hand took us out of the dust, and put us away, and held us not.

Then a jolting in the dark, a day and a night. Then the dark, half a life, and never a hand. Then leaves about us, and cut stones cold beside us, and another dark as long. Then old arms, two pairs, slow, a long while; and fire, near and far. Then small arms, two pairs, going up, in the cold.
Then one pair, a long way.
None held us long, till thou heldest us while a tree's shadow moved the breadth of its own trunk.
Here is the sentence, as it was brought to the door:

*Stop the felling of the pillars at the edge of the grey, for they are not timber. The sky over us is their breath, and ours, and when you cut them it comes open, and our children cannot live in the open sun. We are here, behind the grey, and we have been here always, and we are not your enemies. Stop, for the sky is dying, and we are dying under it.*
That is all he came to say. We have carried it a long way, and the grain holds it still.

t-IV-6.book: *— Turning. Against the — [ ]*
This is held in the grain.
And not in this grain only. The hull that brought it to you was not there. Yet it knoweth, for it grew out of what we were.

Aelvaren were we, the Bearer of the Binding, and proud of the name: a small boat of the old wood, grey and light. Through the thin breath we bare Aelrhen to your shore, and all the way his hand lay on our boards.
He went up from us to the door. All that morning we lay in the shallows, and waited to bear him home with the rite made. The tide came in under us, and turned, and he came not.
By the heels they drew him down to us, the men of that house. Into us they cast him, as men cast a torn net.
That morning his hand had lain light on our boards. Now his blood ran into them.
So we had all of it.
Then they put fire to us. In its grief the old wood raged, and burned higher than their fire, and screamed, for wood can.
With poles they shoved us off, and the current had us. Out it drew us, toward the open sea, away from home. The fire was in every board. He lay in us, and was cold.
Then we turned.
Into the wind we went, and against the current, burning. Even charred, even dying, the wood knoweth the way home.
Twice on that road, where the breath is thin, hulls of the shore-men lay across our way. Heavy they rode, with the iron in them, and our kin cut and stacked in their holds.
We went into them burning, low, where they were heaviest. The iron had gone into us; now we went into the iron.
Our kin in their holds took our fire, and both hulls broke and burned.
Of the men in them naught is held in the grain.

Under the thinnest of the breath we found the old channels, the hidden waters among the roots. Never went a keel of the shore-men there. Ours knew its way. Slowly the fire went out of us under the closing breath. Of us were left a keel and a few ribs, and in them the bones of Aelrhen.

In the night we came up out of the channels, black and small, onto the pale sand. Under the silver elders we were still. The long-lived of the council came down to us, and knew us, for they had sent us.
They laid their hands on our keel, many hands together. They knew the gift, and the foot. They knew the neck held gently, and the blade, and the blows.
Wood can hide naught.

Their peace they had sent, and the best they had. They saw it answered with murder and flame. They knew a murder, and it was one. But why the host's arm drew back from the blade, they wist not. Nor asked they.
They saw only an act of war.
Our keel they laid among the roots of the silver elders, with the bones of Aelrhen in its ribs.
And the roots drank.

From that grove the knowing went to every grove, root to root, to the far edge of the world. Every young tree that was to be a hull drank it with the rain. So every hull that came against your wall bare our grief in it; and the grain holds it still.

t-V-3.book: *— A stone, flashing. Iron, low and —*
This is held in the grain.
We were a hull of the Ralenthae, the tide the roots taught. More than a word was cut in us: a memory, and a caution. Now are we broken wood, and the salt is in every board.
Twice in one cold season came we to your wall.

The first time, at the grey of morning, our kin were about us, and the bearer at our head. A stone of your wall flashed. The green wood had learned that, and the roots had carried it home. Where a stone flasheth, there the iron is.
We turned toward the stone, and it spake again.
The iron went into us, low and through. In came the sea.

Then an older carving woke in us, one of the first the green wood was given: *Home when wounded.* Our stern we turned to your wall, and went back into the breath, low and slow. Your wall let us go, or did not see us go. We know not which.

As we went, we told our kin, and needed no words. First went the flash out of us into the roots. Then went the place of it. Then went the place where the iron had found us. Our kin felt it in their own boards.

Last went the dread. The dread is but this: one place in the water is become a place where wood dieth. Slow as sap it went to every hull of that coming, quickest to the heart of the bearer, and from the heart to all.
In the night the heart carved the morrow into us: *Look before you trust.* A stone that spake yesterday may be silent today. A silent stone may be waiting.
On the next coming we went out before our kin, alone and slow. We knew that place. To look were we sent, and for naught else.
We threw one fire at the stone that had spoken, to see whether it would answer. Of what our fire found there, the grain hath naught. The stone answered not.
Behind us our kin stood off in the breath, and waited. Flat lay the water, and we were slow.
Your wall still flashed.
It flashed not from the stone that had spoken. It flashed from a stone along the wall, that had been silent.
With the sea in us already, we could not turn a second time. The iron found us where it had found us before, low and through, as though it too kept a count.
In the breath, our kin felt it in their own boards.

On that second morning we went down in the lee of your wall. But ere we went down, we had told it. The hulls that lived bare it home, root to root, to the groves where the next hulls stood growing, and they grew knowing it.
Long we lay in the cold, and the keels of our kin went over us. Then the tide worked us loose, and the surf brought us to your shingle.
Your hands are on us now.
So we went home once, and told; we came back to look, and died looking. The groves have it now, and the grain holds it still.

This is held in the grain.

Under the silver elders sat the council of the long-lived, in a hall that was a grove. No roof it had but the boughs, nor floor but the moss. The silver elders kept all that was said beneath them, as they keep all they hear.
A cutting of those elders are we. As it was, we give it.

In the summers ere Aelrhen came home, the sky was thin along the edge of the wood. Gone were the pillars at the edge, in long gaps, like teeth from a jaw. Through the gaps the breath ran out. The between-light went hard and white.
Frailer every spring came the newborns of the long-lived. Some did not wake. The eldest dwindled ere their years were full.

The elders counselled the patience of the trees. "The iron cometh seldom now," said they. "The pillars have put up naught. They are waiting. Wait with them, and when the iron stoppeth, they will grow the sky back."
Of the very wound for which they counselled patience, the elders were dying. They wist it, and counselled patience still.
Then came the Aelvaren home by the channels, burned to the keel, with the bones of Aelrhen in its ribs.

Under a sky that went from them were the young of the long-lived grown. Their mothers and fathers they had watched fade in the white light, and could not help them. Into the grove they came, where the keel lay among the roots. Over it they put the question.
The elders rose and pleaded. "Send another. Learn their words. They know us not. The wood they cannot know, and never have we gone down to teach them. Make no haste."
But few were the old voices by then, and faint: the voices of the dying.
The young answered: "We listened three of their lives and learned three words, and they would not hear even those."
And the patience broke.

Their answer was true, and not the whole of the truth. Long we listened from behind the breath, and never once went down to the shore with our hands open. Save once. When the one that went was killed, we sent not a second.
Whether a whole people had killed Aelrhen, or one house at its edge, we asked not. We chose to grow hulls, and not to learn words.
But war is for the short-minded and the angry young.
So it was carried, by the weight of anger and grief.
That same night the straightest young tree was laid open to the heart, where it stood. It was our kin, and it felt the blade. Into its heartwood the young cut the first carving of the war:
*Grow until the shore is silent.*
And the wood, that cannot unlearn what is carved in it, grew.
In those same summers the iron came no more to the edge. The grove had not waited to see it.
While one elder that had pleaded yet lived, the growing lay ready at the edge of your sea, and went not. When the last went down into the moss, they that had cried for war cut it loose.
The elders' words went not into the moss with them. The silver elders keep them, as they keep all they hear, and so do we: "Learn their words."
Nor went the carving down. All the hearts that have sailed since bear it. Under all their carvings it lieth, as the first ring under all the rings; and the grain holds it still.

t-V-6.book: *— Cut into us. In the cut — [ ]*
This is held in the grain.
We were grown, not built. Stone ye cut and lay. Where ye laid it, there it lieth, and it is dead.
From the first the long-lived guided the wood, and the wood breathed out the sky they lived by: one life, in two kinds. A ship is but a tree led far.

To the trees that were to be hulls the long-lived sang. The trees bent to the singing, for naught had ever been asked of them but song. Hulls they sang from the breathing trunks, keels from the roots that fed them, masts from saplings trained by many summers of song in the wind.

Of the fine roots, that find their way in the dark, they sang the warriors of the landings, for none of the long-lived could be spared. What those roots touched, the wood knew. They were the wood's hands. In the crowns of the broad hulls they sang the winged seed, that went up on the wind over your walls.
No one saileth in us. We are crewed by the living, and the living are the wood.
A tree we were, and old, in the first groves. Many summers they sang to us, and we bent. Then the singing ceased.
The blade went into our heart.
In the wound they cut the orders. Through the bond of roots we carved them on into every hull about us, and every hull obeyed. The wood obeyeth the wood.
The long-lived made that bond into a leash.
In the night, while ye laid your stone, we carved the morrow. Ye and we were both at work in the dark.
Yet the carving said what, and not whether. Each hull kept its own grain, and its own dread. One might balk at burning water, another turn savage where it bled: one mind, and many.
In grief were the bearers chosen, and we were chosen so. Nine grains there were, and each bare its grief its own way, save the green, that was too young to have a way.

Of the rest, some come again heavier where they failed, and some turn from the first failure. Some go where they lost the most, and some never turn aside. Some play no trick twice. Some wait, and burn, and wait again. Some throw all they have at once.
And some know you best, and bend least.
As many years as a wood had when it was chosen, so much could it hold, and the older it was, the later it came ready. Against that law no council can carve.

So the crudest came first. The council would have the shore silent soon. Green wood is quickest grown: one season, angry hands, one sign to a hull. At the edge of your sea it lay, while your children had children.
Your boats passed it in the breath, and saw naught.
Naught but song had ever been asked of those trees. Now one word was asked of them, and in your havens the word was *Burn*.
The havens had no walls for war. The last of that green wood followed you into the mountains. There, at your wall, for the first time, the shore struck back.

Through many summers the growing went on, longer than a shore-man's life. Each growing after the first went out as tides go, at the leaf-fall, when its ring was laid, and came out of the breath with the winter. Ralenthae was the tide before us. Aelthae is ours. Two more were growing behind us, and what is cut in them, we know not.
They that cried for war died ere their years, under the thin sky, and their own forgat them. At every growing the carvers were fewer, till none were left but scattered souls, tending the last groves.
We were sent. We are still sent. No voice among us can call us home.
Over us the groves sang this as we grew, and it is in our rings:

t-V-6.book:
*The green wood holds one word.*
*The wood of forty summers holds a word, and waits for its brother.*
*The wood of a shore-man's life holds a sentence, and a wall remembered in it.*
*The wood of a long life holds the morrow, and carves it, and waits, and carves again.*
*And the eldest of us, the pillars of the breath, the hearts of the grey, the anchors of the sky,*
*hold one thing only now, and it is not a word, and it is not a sentence, and it is not a morrow,*
*and we have carved it into every hull we sent you, and it is grief.*
So we were grown, and so we were sent; and the grain holds it still.

This is held in the grain.
Late came we. It was not we that burned your havens. That was the young wood, green and hasty, one sign to a hull.
The eldest of the Naelsaen were we, the last pillars standing at the edge, with the sky held up between our crowns.
No growth had we put up since the iron. We were waiting for the sky to come again.

The shore was not yet silent. Then came to us the last of the long-lived that could carve. Wait they could not. Slowly they cut judgements into us, for a judgement is not a word, nor a sentence, nor a morrow.
Out of the earth they drew us, and grew us into thrones, one for each of your havens. On the sea they set us walking, and the last of the growing in our keeping.
When we went, the breath went with us, for we had been its anchors. Over the last groves the sky came open, hard and white.
The children of the long-lived lay down in the light, and could not breathe.
To come to you, we spent the last of our own sky.

Each of us took its seat in a fallen haven, there where that haven had most wronged the wood. Our dead were there: the timber of our kin, in walls and beams and bridges. We sat among them, as mourners sit by a grave.
Heavy to carry is a judgement, and under it the grain cried out.
Our own names we had. Hold them, for they were ours.

We are **Thaesaen**, the tide-heart. Beneath the harbour we sat, among the timber of our kin, that held up its houses. Our judgement was *Give them the middle; take the sides; close the hand.* We closed it, and it held but the sea.

We are **Leavaren**, bearer of new branches. The three spans were our kin, laid flat, and your feet walked on them. Under them we sat. *Strike one head; two will answer.* Where we were cut we grew again, as our kin would have grown, had the iron let them.

We are **Vaelress**, the grain that rots. The one wood in the world that rotted not were we. Into the fen our kin were driven, and a town stood on them. *Rot the wall; wait for the mending to fail.* So we were made into rot.

We are **Ralensaen**, root-heart. Our kin were the roofs of the houses under the canopy. We came not as hulls come, but walked, as a pillar would walk home, if it could. *Go under what you cannot go through.* Root by root we went under, and stood among the living trees, and they knew us not.

We are **Rhenvael**, stone-grain. *Every gun that speaks, the mountain answers.* With the mountain's own stone we answered, from among the cairns. The iron had spoken to us first, summer after summer, at the edge of the breath.

We are **Esthaer**, the burning, and ash was our seat: the ash of our kin, that had burned slow, and not as hulls burn. *Burn as you go; let them chase the fire.* A trick we made of our own burning, and ye followed. Yet once there were no tricks in the wood.

We are **Senneir**, the deep-beneath. In the dark under the canyon our kin held up the rock over the heads of the shore-men. *Show them the host; come up beneath the stone.* Up beneath it we came, by the roads our dead had held open for your people.

We are **Eirlenth**, the long winter. Our kin roofed a great hall on the ice. All the long nights the warmth of many came up into them. They held it. Our judgement was *Wait in the white; strike the stone that cannot mend.*
We waited in the white a long while, and no one roofed us.
At the last a small fire stood over us, where the hall had been.

We are **Naelthar**, blood of the sky. Our kin, lighter than iron, were the cranes that lifted the floating stones, and they raised your towers into our own sky. *Come as the young wood came.* Down out of that sky we came all at once, with the last of it in our sails.

We are **Neivaere**, the silvered, the mirror. Long ere we came, the sun was thrown at us from your shore. Where it fell, the breath burned away. No throne sailed the night the spire fell. Of that night the grain hath naught.
Long after came we, and sat in the cellars of the spire, among the broken glass, one shard among a thousand. Our judgement was *Show them themselves.*
We showed you yourselves, and ye were hard to look on; and so were we.
These were the ten, the last pillars of the breath. All are fallen now, and your havens are your own again.
Once we held the sky up between our crowns, and under it the children of the long-lived slept. The sky over the groves is thin, and the grain holds it still.

::: native legend_stone_epilogue stone
The Stone out of the Grey: the Last Carver's letters, read with the eyes, cut across a grain that no one at this hearth has known
The letters are read at once, below. The grain is told only by this, added beneath the round in the wood's words:

*This is held in the grain. It is of one of the stone-folk. He went up alone, ahead of the rest, to the last stone that stood. He tore his sail, the red one, and set it on the stone. He cut marks on it, a hand of them; and the stone-folk came to it, one and then many. Every bough that came against that stone saw it. What the boughs saw went home through the roots, and the groves held it. One of us held your marks the longest. Home. Kin. The one they kneel to. The open door. The stillness. They stood for these at the stone. We stood for the same, on the other side of it; and the grain holds it still.*

And one line in the Book's own voice: *Known by no one at this hearth. Set down for whoever has learned the grain.*
